questions.question: Q: Describe how freeze-thaw weathering works.

points.text: Water enters cracks in rock. When temperature drops below freezing, the water expands by ~9% as it turns to ice, exerting pressure on the crack walls. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles gradually widen the crack until fragments of rock break off.

questions.question: Q: How does hydrolysis weather feldspar?

points.text: Water reacts with feldspar minerals in granite, breaking their chemical bonds and converting them into clay minerals (kaolinite) plus dissolved silica and potassium/sodium ions. This weakens the rock and is a major process in granite weathering.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?

points.text: Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rock where it sits (no transport involved). Erosion is the removal and transport of weathered material by agents such as water, wind or ice.

questions.question: Q: What factors control the rate of weathering?

points.text: Climate (temperature and moisture: warm and wet accelerates chemical weathering; cold promotes freeze-thaw), rock type and mineralogy (some minerals weather faster than others), surface area (more joints = faster weathering), time, and vegetation cover.

questions.question: Q: Describe the layers (horizons) in a typical soil profile.

points.text: O horizon: organic layer (leaf litter). A horizon: topsoil with organic matter and minerals. B horizon: subsoil with accumulated leached minerals (clay, iron). C horizon: partially weathered parent rock (regolith).
